status: candidate / pending_human_review (model reading; not a gate decision)
statement_tested: Measures that load the system (diffusion microstructure, task-evoked electrophysiology, dual-task performance) separate MCI from its matched non-impaired comparator in the very studies where the corresponding macrostructural volume, static structural index or unloaded behavioural measure does not; the dissociation is reported as a within-study head-to-head.

verdicts.reason: Part upheld from the PDF. The groups are matched: age, sex and education do not differ (Table 1, p.4). In Abeta-neg MCI vs NC, FA is lower in 14 of 20 ROIs and MD higher in 16 of 20 (Figure 2 superscript a; p.4). VBM: 'In the Abeta-neg MCI group, an atrophy trend was observed ... however, these changes did not reach statistical significance' (p.5). The authors state the split themselves: 'significant WM damage in both Abeta-pos and Abeta-neg MCI groups, while notable GM atrophy was only observed in the Abeta-pos MCI group' (p.7). So the within-study, same-participant diffusion-vs-volume dissociation is shown. Not yes, for five reasons. (1) It holds only in the 19-patient Abeta-neg subgroup; in Abeta-pos MCI VBM separates (bilateral hippocampus, left parahippocampus), so the static measure does not fail for MCI in general. (2) WM tract diffusion is set against voxelwise GM volume, which is not the corresponding structure; no WM volume is analysed. (3) The arms are tested at different stringency: whole-brain voxelwise FWE, against 20 atlas ROIs with FDR (Methods p.3) or Bonferroni (Figure 2 caption), an internal inconsistency. The VBM null is a threshold null. (4) No measure-by-group test. (5) The comparison is cross-sectional, and not all NCs had PET. Independence: BABRI, Beijing, with no overlap with any supporter or candidate. Its tensor DTI is the same method family as P-666 (round 20: no).

Part upheld from the PDF. Straight-walking velocity (p = 0.780) and cadence (p = 0.247) do not separate 25 MCI from 30 HC; curve-walking velocity (p = 0.007) and cadence (p = 0.018) do (Table 2, p.6). The authors report this themselves: 'we noted no significant deviations between MCI and HC groups during straight walking when assessing macro gait markers such as average velocity and cadence ... curved walking illuminated notable disparities ... even for these macro gait markers' (p.11). Age (p = 0.091) and sex (p = 0.216) are matched, and BMI, education and GDS are adjusted. Not yes, for four reasons. (1) The load is path geometry in a single-task walk, and the authors say the study 'did not incorporate dual-task walking tests' (p.11). This is outside the three named families, so it fits only if that list is illustrative, which is an operator scope decision. (2) The unloaded test itself separates the groups: 20 of 50 straight-walking markers differ, including step and stride length (p = .003, .006), and straight walking gives AUC 0.78 (p.10). The insensitivity is marker by marker, not test by test. (3) About 100 tests are run with no correction. The claim that the curve AUC is 'significantly higher' carries no test statistic. (4) The HC straight velocity SD of 27.92 is anomalous, although the step and stride velocity nulls (p = 0.574, 0.177) carry the null on their own. Independence: IDAA, Semnan, Iran, with no overlap.

Refuted. (1) The authors' own result is that the unloaded measure separates the groups: 'Significant differences were observed in gait speed, stride length and DTC of gait speed between the cognitively normal and MCI group across all 4 tasks' (p.4). Single-task speed is 1.11 vs 0.95 m/s (t = -4.564, p < .001) and single-task stride length differs at p < .001 (Table 3). The study shows that dual-task gait is more sensitive, not that the static measure fails. (2) The only split is single-task cadence at p = .077 against dual-task cadence at p < .001. That is a table-level observation the authors neither state nor test, with no task-by-group test for cadence. (3) The comparator is not matched. The MCI group is older (p = .013), more female (p = .047), shorter (p = .010) and less educated (p < .001) (Table 1), and the Table 3 tests are unadjusted. Shorter stature raises cadence, so the marginal single-task cadence null may be confounded. (4) The MCI dual-task cadence SD roughly doubles (20.68-21.67 vs 11.55 single-task), which is consistent with stopping during the cognitive task. (5) The abstract gives 69/65 while Table 1 gives 62/62. Plus-minus glyphs were decoded from the paper's section-sign 'M-SD' convention; the verdict does not depend on them. Independence: the parent institution (HUST Tongji) is shared with P-666, but the cohort, recruitment route and period differ, and no authors are shared.

Part upheld from the tables. For whole-WM ROI, CN vs EMCI, the f-index gives t = -6.822, p < 0.001, while fw-FA does not differ (F = 0.101, p = 0.904) (Table 7, p.16). WM volume CN-EMCI gives Dunn Z = 0.54, p = 1.00 (Table 8). So a spatially matched diffusion measure separates CN from EMCI where WM volume does not, in the same participants. Not yes, for five reasons. (1) The authors never contrast the two; the dissociation is assembled by the reader. Their own summary reads the static measures as separating: 'Volumetric analyses revealed reduced white and gray matter volumes and increased CSF volumes in the MCI groups' (p.17). (2) GM volume (Z = 4.35) and CSF volume (Z = -3.92) separate the same CN-EMCI contrast (p < 0.001). (3) The metric that succeeds is the free-water fraction, which the authors tie to CSF increase from neuronal loss (p.2); the tissue metric fw-FA fails at whole-WM level. (4) The arms are analysed differently. The diffusion arm uses ComBat with age, sex and motion plus ANCOVA/Tukey; the volume arm uses unadjusted Kruskal-Wallis/Dunn-Bonferroni on percentage volumes. Sex differs (CN 60% vs EMCI 40% female). (5) The data are single-shell and multi-scanner. The EMCI-vs-LMCI contrast the authors emphasise has no non-impaired comparator. The ADNI family is not on the record yet, so an all-ADNI declaration is needed only if other ADNI supporters are added.

Refuted. (1) The left fornix is the only tract where MCI as a whole (both subgroups) differs from HC-NA (mGFA p = .009 and .045, p.6). Its corresponding static measure, hippocampal volume, also separates both MCI groups (right p = .02/.003, left p = .032/.008), and so does right frontal thickness (p = .01/.03) (Section 3.2, p.6). There is no dissociation. (2) The only printed static nulls are the three-group global total cerebral GM (p = 0.10) and WM (p = 0.91) volumes (Table 1), which are not the corresponding measure of any single tract. (3) The best remaining pairing, callosal-IPL mGFA in MCI-PA vs HC-NA (p = .001) against IPL thickness, rests on a null that is never printed: IPL thickness is simply absent from the significant list, and Fig. 1 shows only significant regions. That pairing is also confined to the 22-patient poor-awareness subgroup, an awareness-defined split, and MCI-NA did not differ on that tract. (4) 'These results could not be explained by gray matter morphometric differences' concerns MCI-PA against the other groups, and the two MCI groups had identical morphometry. It is not an MCI-vs-control head-to-head. The brain analyses are uncorrected at p < 0.05. The source does not show a static measure failing where the diffusion measure succeeds for MCI vs a non-impaired comparator.

Refuted. (1) The EEG response is TMS-evoked at rest, not task-evoked: 'To ensure wakefulness, subjects were required to fixate a target over the wall' (p.3). (2) The non-separating measures, RMT (p = 0.87) and MEP amplitude (p = 0.11) (Table 1), are themselves corticospinal responses to the same TMS pulse. The pairing is evoked against evoked, not loaded against a macrostructural volume, static structural index or unloaded behavioural measure. The paper never presents them as a sensitivity contrast. (3) The EEG separation itself is partial. The group main effect on the TEP map is non-significant (F = 0.386, p = 0.54), and ERSP shows no group effect (p = 0.78). GMFP at 45-50 ms (p = 0.045) comes from sample-by-sample t-tests. ITC post hoc p-values are 0.03-0.048 at most channels. What remains is the sensitivity half only, the ground on which round 20 scored P-666 'no'. N = 32, and the authors call the results preliminary.

Part upheld from the PDF. Central RT does not separate the groups: 554.4 vs 568.5 ms, t = -1.22, p = 0.228, d = -0.29. UFOV RT does: 580.3 vs 638.6 ms, t = -5.84, p < 0.001, d = -1.17. The Task x Group interaction is F(1,72) = 19.09, p < 0.001, and the group effect survives central RT as a covariate (F = 37.94) (p.4). Age is matched (p = 0.12, Table 1). This is a formally tested loaded-vs-unloaded behavioural dissociation. Not yes, for three reasons. (1) The UFOV condition is peripheral target detection under central fixation with no concurrent task ('While maintaining gaze on the fixation point, red circular targets ... presented in one of four peripheral locations', p.3). It is not a dual task, and 'dual-task interference' is the authors' Discussion framing (p.7). It fits only if the family list is illustrative, which is an operator scope decision. (2) Confounds: the task order is fixed (central first); there are 20 vs 80 trials; the targets sit 20 cm off-centre at 1 m (about 11 deg), so eccentricity and sensory or oculomotor costs are not excluded (no visual-field test); visual orienting frequency is higher in MCI at trend level (p = 0.052). (3) Groups are defined only by MoCA-J/MMSE-J, which the authors call provisional; single site. Independence: Kyoto/Osaka facilities, with no overlap.

Refuted. Electrophysiology limb: there is no ERP group main effect. The P2 and P3 differences are group x load x surprise interactions (F = 9.41, 9.17, p.5). The single group main effect is microstate B GFP (F = 7.82, p < .01), which the authors relate to the visual evoked potential. The measure that fails is RT on the same task (F = 1.07, p = .31), while accuracy on the same task separates the groups (F = 5.12, p < .05). That is a neural versus same-task-behaviour pattern with no static counterpart. The Stroop null (p = .10, Table 1) is never paired with the EEG. So this limb shows only the sensitivity half (P-666 precedent: no). Behavioural limb: there is a load x group accuracy interaction (F = 4.51, p < .05; high load 94 vs 96%, p < .05; low load p = .14). But low-load accuracy is at ceiling (99%, SD 1%), so the unloaded null cannot demonstrate insensitivity. The overall accuracy group effect is itself significant. The load is arrow-congruency difficulty within one perceptual task, not a dual task, and the effect is 2 points. The source does not show the loaded-versus-static dissociation. No verdict depends on Elsevier glyphs. Independence: Shenzhen University community screening. Its sibling Guan-lab paper P-433 is neither a supporter nor a candidate.

tally.method: Independent yes supporters, counting each dataset family once. Round-20 per-supporter readings are combined with the candidates that survive Step 1. Only 'yes' counts; 'partly' does not.

round20_current_supporters.P-687: yes, but the SAME Guangzhou sample as P-665 (identical demographics, TUG values, ethics [2021]475-1): one family, counted once
round20_current_supporters.P-661: partly (no non-impaired comparator; neural vs same-task behaviour)
round20_current_supporters.P-666: no (sensitivity half only; no static comparator)

Guangzhou sample, First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University, 30 MCI / 30 HC (P-665 and P-687 report the same participants)

tally.narrowed_note: The round-20 narrowed wording declares VF-25 not a convergence and names only the P-651 and Guangzhou samples. Every candidate is n/a under it, so the narrowed count stays at two.

scope_note_for_operator: Two partly candidates (P-1082 curve walking, P-1163 UFOV reaction time) show a loaded-versus-unloaded behavioural dissociation with a load that is not a dual task. Whether 'diffusion microstructure, task-evoked electrophysiology, dual-task performance' is an exhaustive list or illustrative is a question about the statement's scope. This reading does not decide it. Under the wording as written, both are partly. P-1082 would stay partly even under a broader reading, because straight walking as a test separates the groups (AUC 0.78). No candidate supplies the missing electrophysiology dissociation.
summary: None of the eight candidates is a yes under the stated form. Four keep partly (P-1425, P-1082, P-566, P-1163) and four drop to no (P-604, P-473, P-522, P-633). Combined with round 20, VF-25 has two independent yes samples: P-651 (Chongqing CSVD) and one Guangzhou sample reported twice (P-665, P-687). The stated form does not reach three, and the narrowed wording, which is not a convergence, stays at two.
